title: Relationships
summary: Model relationships (one-to-one, one-to-many with ForeignKey, many-to-many), splitting code into separate Django apps, how the Django server turns a request into a response, and passing parameters through URL patterns. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Connect Django models with relationships and route URLs with parameters to views that return responses.

steps.title: Find the relationships in your Netflix schema
steps.detail: Your migrations already have all three kinds. One-to-one: `profiles.id references auth.users (id)`. One-to-many: `shows.genre_id references public.genres (id)` (one genre, many shows). Many-to-many: `list_items` joins `lists` and `shows`. Open assignments/week-02/netflix/supabase/migrations/ and find each one.
steps.doneWhen: You can name the table and column behind each of the three relationships.

steps.title: Read Django's relationship fields
steps.detail: Read the Relationships section of the Models page: ForeignKey, ManyToManyField and OneToOneField, plus what `on_delete` means (it matches your `on delete cascade`).
steps.doneWhen: You can match each Netflix relationship to the Django field you'd use for it.

steps.title: Read the URL dispatcher example
steps.detail: Read the Example and Path converters parts of Django's URL docs. This is how a URL like /students/5/ reaches a view with id=5.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain what `<int:id>` does in `path('students/<int:id>/', ...)`.

concepts.meaning: A one-to-many link: many rows in one table point at one row in another.
A link where each side can have many of the other, stored in a join table.
What happens to linked rows when the row they point at is deleted (e.g. CASCADE).
A rule in urls.py that maps a URL path to a view.
The browser sends a request; Django runs a view and sends back a response.
